title: Sandbox Workload
description: Sandbox-level view: inventory and lifecycle, the create path, what guests are actually consuming (CPU/memory/disk/network), billable volume, and id resolution. Aggregated across the fleet — no series is labelled with a sandbox id, by design (cardinality); per-sandbox detail is GET /v1/sandboxes/{id}/metrics.

panels.title: Running
panels.description: User-visible running sandboxes, summed from the workers themselves (sandbox_running excludes hidden ready-pool VMs, unlike the gateway's slots_used).

panels.title: Hibernated
panels.description: Frozen to disk: holds a host port and its artifacts, no slot, no memory, no bill.

panels.title: In transition
panels.description: starting + stopping: bring-ups past validation and bounded teardowns. A number that will not fall means a create or destroy is wedged.

panels.title: Ready VMs available
panels.description: Fully initialized hidden clones a create can claim in ~10 ms. Zero means every arrival pays the ~700 ms clone path.

panels.title: Ready VMs preparing
panels.description: Ready-pool builds still completing launch/readiness/security gates; unclaimable.

panels.title: Creates queued
panels.description: Creates parked in the gateway's bounded queue waiting for a slot. Non-zero is the level-triggered scale-out signal.

panels.title: Sandbox inventory
panels.description: User inventory (running, hibernated) plus transient worker states and hidden ready-pool VMs. Warm series are not user sandboxes but do consume slots and memory.

panels.title: Lifecycle events (events/min)
panels.description: Arrival and freeze/thaw churn. Wake failures roll a sandbox back to hibernated and surface to the client as 503 (or close code 4503 on the shell WebSocket).

panels.title: Create success (1h)
panels.description: Worker bring-ups that succeeded, of those attempted past validation. Capacity 503s are not counted here — see the rejection rate.

panels.title: Ready-pool hit rate (1h)
panels.description: Creates served from a ready VM rather than the clone fallback. This is the difference between a ~10 ms create and a ~700 ms one; size warm_pool_size off it.

panels.title: Capacity rejections (5m)
panels.description: Creates 503'd because the queue was full or the queue wait expired. Retrying clients re-increment every Retry-After, so read it as demand the queue can no longer express.

panels.title: Worker create errors (5m)
panels.description: Bring-ups that failed after validation: agent-readiness timeout, clone failure, jailer/device problem. A non-zero count with free capacity is a host defect, not load.

panels.title: Golden-ready workers
panels.description: Workers with the golden snapshot staged. A worker without it cold-boots every create (~2 s) instead of cloning.

panels.title: Create outcomes (events/min)
panels.description: Successful creates versus the two failure classes. Capacity rejections are the gateway's; create errors are the workers'.

panels.title: Ready pool
panels.description: Claims versus misses is the hit rate over time; build failures mean the pool cannot refill and every subsequent arrival falls back to the clone path.

panels.title: Queue and admission pressure
panels.description: Queue depth is a request count; demand slots weight memory-heavy requests the way the gateway's own scaling arithmetic does. In-flight versus the per-host concurrency ceiling shows whether workers are the bottleneck rather than capacity.

panels.title: Mean sandbox CPU
panels.description: Mean of per-sandbox CPU used as a percentage of its OWN allocated vCPUs, so 100% means a sandbox is using everything it was given.

panels.title: Idle sandboxes (≤1%)
panels.description: Resident sandboxes doing essentially nothing. They still hold a slot, a tap/IP and committed memory, so a large number is the case for a shorter hibernate_after_sec.

panels.title: Busy sandboxes (>75%)
panels.description: Sandboxes near or at their vCPU allocation. CPU is deliberately oversubscribed ~6:1, so this is where contention shows up first.

panels.title: Sampled sandboxes
panels.description: Sandboxes in the utilization histogram. The sampler reads the cgroup leaf, tap counters and rootfs file — never the guest — so it neither counts as activity nor wakes a hibernated sandbox.

panels.title: Guest telemetry coverage
panels.description: Running sandboxes whose agent answered GET /stats, over all running. Below 1 means some guests carry an agent predating /stats (image-pinned — rebake) and the guest-reported panels below cover only part of the fleet.

panels.title: Per-sandbox CPU utilization percentiles
panels.description: Quantiles over the current population of sandboxes (a snapshot distribution, not a rate — the buckets are gauges reset each scrape). p99 pinned at 100% with a low mean is a few busy tenants, not a hot fleet.

panels.title: CPU utilization distribution (share of sandboxes)
panels.description: How the population splits by utilisation band. The idle band is the density opportunity; the top band is the contention risk.

panels.title: Memory: allocated vs touched vs in use
panels.description: Three different numbers, and the gap between them is the whole overcommit case. Allocated is what admission charges (effective mem_mib + 156 MiB VMM overhead). Touched is the VMM cgroup charge, a high-water mark that never falls without a balloon device. In use is what the guest itself reports free/used — the only one that drops when a workload finishes.

panels.title: Guest memory in use
panels.description: Guest-reported used over total, across sandboxes that answered /stats. This is memory pressure inside the sandboxes, which the host's cgroup charge cannot see.

panels.title: Guest disk in use
panels.description: Guest-reported rootfs used over total. A sandbox that fills its disk fails in confusing ways (npm installs, git clones) long before anything else alarms.

panels.title: Memory touched per sandbox
panels.description: Mean VMM cgroup charge per running sandbox — the density figure to watch across releases (snapshot-sourced sandboxes share golden pages and measure well below default-sourced ones).

panels.title: Mean guest load / processes
panels.description: Per reporting sandbox: 1-minute load average and process count. Load above the sandbox's vCPU count means work is queueing inside the guest.

panels.title: Guest network throughput
panels.description: From the guest's point of view (the tap's counters are swapped on the way in). Egress leaves via host NAT, so this is also the fleet's outbound bill.

panels.title: Rootfs growth
panels.description: Only the GROWTH is the sandboxes' own consumption: the absolute sum counts the ~2.2 GiB reflinked golden base once per sandbox, so watch the slope, not the level.

panels.title: Telemetry gaps (events/min)
panels.description: Utilization ticks where a running guest did not answer /stats: an agent predating the endpoint, a timeout, or an unreachable guest. Host-side fields still record; the guest-reported panels above lose coverage.

panels.title: Billed vCPU rate
panels.description: Allocated vCPU-seconds per second credited as intervals close — effectively the vCPU count the fleet is charging for. Billing is on ALLOCATION, not consumption.

panels.title: Billed memory rate
panels.description: Allocated GiB credited per second as intervals close.

panels.title: CPU oversubscription
panels.description: Allocated vCPU-seconds over consumed CPU seconds, both credited at interval close. ~6:1 is the intended design point; near 1:1 means guests are actually using their allocation and contention is real.

panels.title: Open intervals vs running
panels.description: One open billable interval per running sandbox's VMM. A persistent gap either way means the ledger and the inventory disagree.

panels.title: Unflushed intervals
panels.description: Closed billing evidence that exists only on a worker's local disk. Alert on this: a scale-in that deletes the instance destroys it, and the bucket — not SQLite — is the billing record.

panels.title: Billable volume over time
panels.description: Allocated versus consumed, on the same axis in vCPU terms. Both are credited when an interval CLOSES, so a fleet of long-lived sandboxes shows these move in steps.

panels.title: Usage ledger health
panels.description: Open intervals should track running inventory; unflushed intervals should return to zero after each spool to the durability bucket.

panels.title: Routes vs inventory
panels.description: The gateway rebuilds sandbox-id → host routing from heartbeats and holds no durable state. Routes should track running + hibernated; a shortfall is a sandbox nobody can reach, an excess is a stale route.

panels.title: Cross-host adopt (events/min)
panels.description: A route miss is resolved by asking workers, and that probe is RATE-LIMITED: rising `throttled` with a low dispatch rate means something is probing ids, while rising wait timeouts means real adopts are slower than clients wait and 404s are being returned for sandboxes that exist.

panels.title: Wake latency, public ingress (seconds)
panels.description: Measured at the edge: a request to a hibernated sandbox's public port thaws it before proxying. Only ingress-driven wakes are timed — API-driven wakes are not instrumented.

panels.title: What is and is not here

options.content:
**No sandbox-id labels, deliberately.** Every series is a host aggregate; a `sandbox_id` label at this
churn rate is a cardinality bomb. Per-sandbox history lives in a bounded in-memory ring on the owning
worker and is read with `GET /v1/sandboxes/{id}/metrics` (`sandbox metrics <id>`) — lost on restart and
when a sandbox moves hosts.

**Allocation vs consumption.** *Billed* series are ALLOCATION (`vcpus`/`mem_mib` × duration) and are
credited when an interval closes, so they move in steps. *Utilization* series are what a guest is
actually using, sampled every 5 s. They are not meant to match.

**Guest-reported panels depend on the baked agent.** `metrics_guest_stats` polls each guest's
`GET /stats`; an agent predating it degrades silently to host-only fields. The coverage stat and
`sandbox_guest_stat_failures_total` are how you see that — the agent is image-pinned, so the fix is a
rebake, not a rollout.

**Gaps.** There is no create-latency histogram (the 12 ms / 700 ms figures come from benchmark runs,
not from this dashboard), no per-sandbox network or disk quota accounting, and no API request-rate or
error-rate series for exec/files/shell.

**A slow create** → *Create path*. Ready-pool hit rate near zero means arrivals are paying the clone
fallback; that is pool sizing (`warm_pool_size`), not a defect. Queue depth above zero with rejections
means the fleet is short of capacity — continue on **Sandbox Hosts** (scaling row).

**A sandbox that feels starved** → *Guest CPU*. Compare p99 against the mean: a pinned p99 with a low
mean is a few tenants at their own vCPU ceiling, which oversubscription cannot fix for them. Check
mean guest load against vCPUs allocated.

**A worker OOM or admission 503** → *Guest memory*. `allocated` is what admission charges against
`mem_budget_mib`; `touched` is what the host is really paying. A large gap is headroom a balloon device
could reclaim (see CLAUDE.md, "No memory overcommit").

**Missing money** → *Billable volume*. Unflushed intervals above zero for more than a spool cycle is
the one to page on: a scale-in deleting that instance destroys the evidence.

**A 404 for a sandbox that exists** → *Id resolution*. 404 from the gateway is supposed to mean a
proven absence; rising adopt wait timeouts or `suppressed{reason="throttled"}` is how that guarantee
degrades under bulk churn.
